items.question: Explain what is meant by a magnetic circuit. Which materials are used to build one, and why?
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: A magnetic circuit is the closed path followed by magnetic flux lines. It is made of high-permeability materials such as soft steel or iron, which offer low resistance to flux, and is used in motors, transformers and generators.
items.original_question: What is a magnetic circuit?

items.question: Define MMF. On which two quantities does it depend?
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: MMF is the magnetic pressure responsible for setting up magnetic flux in a magnetic circuit. It is the product of the number of turns N of the coil and the current I through it (ampere-turns).
items.original_question: Define magnetomotive force (MMF).

items.question: What opposes the setting up of flux in a magnetic circuit, and which physical factors decide its value?
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Reluctance is the opposition offered by a magnetic circuit to the production of magnetic flux, analogous to resistance. It depends on the length, the cross-sectional area and the permeability of the material: S = l/(a*mu), measured in AT/Wb.
items.original_question: What is reluctance and on what factors does it depend?

items.question: Why is the magnetisation curve of a ferromagnetic material not a straight line?
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: The B-H (magnetisation) curve plots flux density B against magnetising force H and shows how B varies with H. It is non-linear because the relative permeability of a magnetic material is not constant but varies with flux density.
items.original_question: What does the B-H curve show and why is it not a straight line?

items.question: Distinguish between residual magnetism and coercive force of a ferromagnetic material.
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Retentivity is the magnetisation (B) that remains when the external magnetising field is removed. Coercivity is the reverse magnetising field (-H) needed to demagnetise the material completely.
items.original_question: What is the difference between retentivity and coercivity?

items.question: Why does a transformer core heat up due to repeated magnetisation, and how is this loss kept small?
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Hysteresis loss is the energy lost as heat during repeated magnetisation and demagnetisation; the loss per unit volume equals the area of the hysteresis loop. Transformers use a soft iron core because its hysteresis loss is much smaller.
items.original_question: What is hysteresis loss and how is it reduced in transformers?

items.question: Give points of difference between magnetic circuits and electric circuits.
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Flux = MMF/reluctance versus current = EMF/resistance; flux in webers versus current in amperes; MMF in ampere-turns versus EMF in volts; there is no perfect magnetic insulator; reluctance varies with B while resistance is almost constant; energy is needed only to set up flux, but continuously for current.
items.original_question: Compare a magnetic circuit with an electric circuit.

items.question: Name and briefly describe the main parts of a DC machine.
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Yoke, poles and pole shoes, field winding, armature core, armature winding, and commutator with brushes.
items.original_question: What are the main constructional parts of a DC machine?

items.question: Why is a commutator needed in a DC generator?
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: It collects the current from the armature conductors and acts as a mechanical rectifier, converting the alternating current induced in the armature into direct current at the load terminals through stationary brushes.
items.original_question: What is the function of the commutator in a DC generator?

items.question: How do the field windings of series and shunt DC generators differ in connection, wire size and resistance?
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Series: field in series with the armature, carries the full load current, few turns of thick wire, very low resistance (about 0.5 ohm). Shunt: field in parallel with the armature, full voltage across it, many turns of thin wire, high resistance (about 100 ohm), takes under 5% of rated current.
items.original_question: Differentiate between series wound and shunt wound DC generators.

items.question: State the generated EMF equation of a DC generator. How does it change for lap and wave windings?
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Eg = P*phi*Z*N / (60*A) volts, where P = poles, phi = flux per pole, Z = armature conductors, N = speed in rpm, A = parallel paths. For lap winding A = P; for wave winding A = 2.
items.original_question: Write the EMF equation of a DC generator.

items.question: What is back EMF? Explain why it makes a DC motor self-regulating.
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Back EMF is the EMF induced in the motor armature by generator action; it opposes the supply voltage, Eb = P*phi*Z*N/(60*A). It is needed for energy conversion (Pmech = Eb*Ia) and regulates armature current, Ia = (V - Eb)/Ra, making the motor self-regulating.
items.original_question: What is back EMF and what is its significance in a DC motor?

items.question: Show that the armature torque of a DC motor is proportional to flux and armature current.
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Ta = 9.55 * Eb * Ia / N = 0.159 * P * phi * Z * Ia / A newton-metres, so torque is proportional to flux times armature current; shaft torque = Ta - frictional torque.
items.original_question: Derive or state the armature torque equation of a DC motor.

items.question: Compare slip-ring and cage-type induction motors in construction, starting torque and applications.
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Slip ring: complicated construction with slip rings and brushes, external rotor resistance can be added, high starting torque, more maintenance, costlier, used in cranes and hoists. Squirrel cage: simple, rugged, cheap, bars shorted by end rings, low starting torque, less maintenance, widely used in fans, lathes and pumps.
items.original_question: What are the differences between slip ring and squirrel cage induction motors?

items.question: Define slip. Why can the rotor of an induction motor never reach synchronous speed?
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Slip s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns. At synchronous speed there is no relative motion between the rotating field and the rotor, so no EMF or current is induced and no torque is produced; the rotor therefore settles below synchronous speed.
items.original_question: What is slip, and why can an induction motor never run at synchronous speed?

items.question: Using double revolving field theory, explain why a single-phase induction motor cannot start on its own.
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: Its stator produces a pulsating, not rotating, field. By double revolving field theory this splits into two equal fields rotating in opposite directions whose torques are equal and opposite at start, so the net starting torque is zero.
items.original_question: Why is a single-phase induction motor not self-starting?

items.question: Why does a synchronous motor fail to start by itself? List the methods used to start it.
items.subject: Electrical Engineering
items.reference_answer: The stator field reverses every half cycle, so the stationary rotor gets a rapidly reversing torque and cannot start. It is started with a pony motor, a damper winding, or a small coupled DC machine that brings it near synchronous speed before DC excitation locks it in.
items.original_question: Why is a synchronous motor not self-starting and what methods are used to start it?

items.question: How does a CV differ from a resume and a biodata?
items.subject: Technical Communication
items.expected_source: Unit 2 communication skills for Career building.pdf
items.reference_answer: A biodata emphasises personal details (age, marital status, etc.) and is now obsolete; a resume omits personal details and is skill-oriented, suited to any position; a CV has everything in a resume plus detailed academic credentials and publications, and is knowledge-oriented for research positions.
items.original_question: What is the difference between a biodata, a resume and a CV?

items.question: Which resume format suits someone who is changing careers, and what other formats are there?
items.subject: Technical Communication
items.expected_source: Unit 2 communication skills for Career building.pdf
items.reference_answer: A functional resume, which focuses on skills and experience rather than chronological work history, is used by people changing careers or with employment gaps. Other formats: chronological (work history in reverse order, for a strong work history), combination (skills first, then employment history) and targeted.
items.original_question: What are the different types of resumes?

items.question: Why might an interviewer deliberately ask rude or rapid-fire questions, and what is this interview called?
items.subject: Technical Communication
items.expected_source: Unit 2 communication skills for Career building.pdf
items.reference_answer: An interview that tests how a candidate responds to aggressive, embarrassing or rude questioning, e.g. several questions at once, no time to answer, an interrogatory tone or unrelated questions, to see how well they work under pressure.
items.original_question: What is a stress interview?

items.question: What should a job applicant do before and during an interview to make a good impression?
items.subject: Technical Communication
items.expected_source: Unit 2 communication skills for Career building.pdf
items.reference_answer: Research the company, look sharp, be prepared with resume copies and questions, be on time, show enthusiasm, listen, answer the question asked, give specific examples, ask questions and follow up afterwards.
items.original_question: How should a candidate prepare for an interview?

items.question: Define a group discussion and describe how it is usually conducted.
items.subject: Technical Communication
items.expected_source: Unit 2 communication skills for Career building.pdf
items.reference_answer: According to R C Sharma and Krishna Mohan, a GD is held to discuss a problem or issue to arrive at a decision and exchange information, and is used to assess a candidate's suitability. Usually 6-10 people (sometimes up to 16), unstructured with no chairperson, lasting 10-15 minutes, with 2-3 minutes thinking time for topics; one or two experts evaluate it.
items.original_question: What is a group discussion, and how many participants does it usually have?

items.question: Why do organisations and trainers use group discussions? State their objectives.
items.subject: Technical Communication
items.expected_source: Unit 2 communication skills for Career building.pdf
items.reference_answer: Produce a range of options or solutions, generate ideas by examining issues in depth, broaden participants' outlook, develop interpersonal communication skills, change attitudes through peer influence, and give the training team feedback on participants.
items.original_question: What are the objectives of a group discussion?

items.question: What behaviour should a candidate avoid during a group discussion?
items.subject: Technical Communication
items.expected_source: Unit 2 communication skills for Career building.pdf
items.reference_answer: Do not initiate without knowledge of the topic, over-speak or snatch others' chances, argue or shout, look at evaluators, talk irrelevantly, use negative body gestures, quote wrong statistics, show low confidence, dominate, or embarrass others.
items.original_question: List the don'ts of participating in a group discussion.

items.question: What is an SOP, and why does it matter when applying to study abroad?
items.subject: Technical Communication
items.expected_source: Unit 2 communication skills for Career building.pdf
items.reference_answer: An SOP is a letter to the admission committee stating why the applicant chose a course, their interests, goals and career plans. It is important because it is often the first document read, makes the application stand out among similar candidates and shows how well the applicant articulates ideas.
items.original_question: What is a Statement of Purpose (SOP) and why is it important?

items.question: Compare a conference and a seminar in terms of purpose, duration and audience participation.
items.subject: Technical Communication
items.expected_source: Unit 2 communication skills for Career building.pdf
items.reference_answer: A conference is a large formal gathering over a few days to discuss a topic of common interest and get opinions or solutions, with limited audience participation. A seminar is an instructional event of an hour or more where one or two experts educate and guide, with active participation.
items.original_question: What is the difference between a conference and a seminar?
